unit: computer-science / computational-thinking (free tier) - lessons 12 and 13 only

findings.claim: Unless a question says you may answer in a high-level language such as Python, write your code in the exam reference language.
findings.truth: The choice is the student's, not the question's. The spec says questions that assess writing or refining algorithms must be answered using either the exam reference language or the high-level programming language the student is familiar with. Telling a student to default to the reference language unless given permission could push them away from the language they know best.
findings.evidence: spec assessment overview, J277/02: 'In Section B, questions assessing students' ability to write or refine algorithms must be answered using either the OCR Exam Reference Language or the high-level programming language they are familiar with.'

findings.claim: Where a question lets you answer in a high-level language, Python does the same jobs with different names.
findings.truth: Same error as F1 in a second place: a question does not have to 'let' a student use a high-level language on a write or refine task; that option is always open.
findings.evidence: spec assessment overview, J277/02 Section B response rules; spec section 3b response tables (Write and Refine: reference language or a high-level programming language)

findings.claim: part of it asks you to design, write, test and refine programs. In that part an answer written as natural English or as bullet points scores nothing
findings.truth: That is true only of the write and refine questions. In the same section, design questions are answered in pseudocode, flowcharts, tick boxes or natural English, and testing questions in trace tables or test plans, all of which earn marks. The spec limits the 'no marks' rule to responses that require the reference language or a high-level language.
findings.evidence: spec section 3b, Section B response table (Design: pseudocode / flowcharts / tick-box / natural English; Test: trace tables / test plans / test data) and the note 'Where a response requires an answer in [the reference language] or a high-level programming language ... Answers written in pseudocode, natural English or bullet points will not be awarded marks.'

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Which keyword names the table a query reads from?' with the answer 'FROM.'
findings.truth: The answer word sits in its own question, so the card gives itself away and tests nothing. Reword the question so it does not contain 'from'.
findings.evidence: house flashcard rule: no answer word in its question

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'What is returned by a SELECT clause that uses a star instead of field names?' with the answer 'Every field in the table.'
findings.truth: The answer word 'field' sits in the question. Cutting the trailing phrase removes the prompt and leaves the card testing the same thing.
findings.evidence: house flashcard rule: no answer word in its question

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Why does a written answer in bullet points score nothing on a programming question?'
findings.truth: Bullet points score nothing only when the question asks for code. On a design question in the same section, bullet points and natural English are accepted answers. The stem needs narrowing to write-a-program questions. Same error class as F3.
findings.evidence: spec section 3b, Section B response table (Design accepts bullet points and natural English)

findings.claim: SQL questions on it are usually worth two to four marks, with one mark for each clause you get right.
findings.truth: The spec sets no mark tariff for SQL questions. The claim is a reasonable teaching heuristic and is hedged with 'usually', so it is not worth an edit, but it is not spec-backed.
findings.evidence: spec section 2.2.3 lists SELECT, FROM and WHERE with no mark tariff; the assessment section gives only Section A 50 marks and Section B 30 marks

findings.claim: not equal to <> is given as the SQL not-equal operator
findings.truth: Correct for SQL, and the spec names no SQL operators at all, so nothing here is wrong. Worth recording only because the spec's own comparison-operator table for code questions uses != for not equal, so a student meets both symbols in the same paper.
findings.evidence: spec section 2.2.1 operator table (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=); spec section 2.2.3 names only SELECT, FROM and WHERE

summary: Every reference-language name, every worked query on the Books and Stock tables, every string and character-code trace, all ten knowledge-check keys and both Paper 2 claims (1 hour 30 minutes, 80 marks) check out against the spec; random(1,6) and random(-1.0,10.0) are the spec's own examples, and the LIKE section is already flagged as beyond the course. The only real error is the lesson 13 claim that a high-level language needs the question's permission, and the linked over-statement that natural English and bullet points never score in the programming section.
